entries.trigger: the class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: The best Hit Points in the book, any armour you can lift, and a 5 to hit — which at skill level I still means three swings in four hit nothing but corridor. Fighters are the only delvers who die of something other than a mistake. A scroll, for you, is an intelligence roll that can backfire — unless you paid for Runes/Signs.

entries.trigger: the class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Twenty-five Hit Points plus whatever the d10 pities you with, a staff you cannot really use, and a 3 to hit — six swings in seven are decorative. Everything you are is in the grimoire. No special skills: the book's position is that spells ought to be enough. Every scroll reads for you without fail — the one roll in the whole dungeon you never have to make.

entries.trigger: the class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Forty Hit Points, leather at the very best, and an opening strike that lands twice as hard as it ought to. Twelve value points of special skills, more than anyone else gets. A thief's plan is to be elsewhere by round three, and thieves are excellent at plans. A scroll is still an intelligence roll that can backfire, no matter how many locks you've picked.

entries.trigger: the race blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Two extra damage, a wilmst a day to feed, and every creature down here swings at you like it has been practising — but your armour shrugs off wear at half the rate everyone else's does, and being small makes you one face harder to hit besides. Built low, built cheap, built to be hit, built to keep the dents. Dwarves call this a fair trade. Dwarves are rarely asked.

entries.trigger: the race blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Thin-boned, easy to hit, and carrying not much more than half a person's Hit Points — but you strike a die better than anyone has a right to, and hit on a 5 whatever the class. Small costs you two points of damage and nothing else; the size rule has nothing left to add to how thin-boned or easy to hit you already were. The elven plan is to kill it before it notices how little you can take. The plan holds until it doesn't.

entries.trigger: the race blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You will not wear armour, though your hide alone soaks two points off every blow that lands. You will not strike first. Five times in eight you lose the plot entirely and swing twice at whatever is nearest — and unlike the stories, neither swing is ever wasted on something already dead. The Game Master has notes about you.

entries.trigger: the race blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: No advantages, no penalties, no excuses. The dungeon keeps humans around the way a kitchen keeps salt — everything else is measured against them. You will die in a manner the Game Master considers statistically unremarkable.

entries.trigger: the race blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Seventy-five Hit Points, +11 damage per swing (nine Troll, two more for being Large), and an appetite that goes through two rations a night. The strongest thing on most floors, one face easier for anything to hit, and the first to starve on all of them. Everything you own cost triple.

entries.trigger: the race blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You heal twice as fast and learn half as quickly, so you will survive a great deal and understand almost none of it. Magic Users despise you on sight — not one of them will so much as travel with you — which most Wilmsry take as proof they are doing something right.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Everything needs a 3 to lay a hand on you and you may carry nothing but a knife. You strike with it like a fighter — nobody armours against a dagger held by someone who will not stand still.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Double experience points until level three, one spell in eight goes off in your hands, and at level three you finally roll to discover what you actually are. Assuming you get there.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Two attacks a round and half the experience points, on the sound principle that a man swinging twice is learning nothing either time.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Five songs, one every hundred squares, and dragons hand over gifts to hear them. Camp for the night and creatures too stupid to know better come looking twice as often, and once the fighting starts they come for you first — which, down here, is most of them.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Your first strike of any fight always lands. You also go through every door first and take the full weight of whatever waits behind it. These two facts are related.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Healing, turning the dead, chain mail and a shield: the one Magic User the dungeon cannot simply push over. A 4 to hit instead of a 3. The gods have rounded up.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You can vanish for free, right up until you land your first blow — after that you flee like everyone else, and you earn precisely nothing from the fight you vanish out of. A Cloaker's career is a long list of encounters that never technically happened.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You talk first, and anything with wit of 6 or under simply declines to fight you. Your first landed blow does no damage at all, because part of you is still hoping to sell them something.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You talk. Through encounters, through corridors, through other people's turns — which means that when a fight actually starts, everyone else gets there first. One creature in six dies of boredom before it comes to that, and the book counts that as a kill.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Double damage on your first landed blow, and Joiners will walk beside you all the same — word travels, but so do they. One descent in twenty, the one beside you does not reach the next floor, and everyone knows why. Nobody has ever asked you to explain. You have never offered.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: No critical strike, ever, and three damage off the top until level four — but every creature down here needs one better than usual to land a blow on you. You are a professional. The profession is standing there.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You choose where the teleport squares put you, which in a dungeon is very close to owning the floor. A Phantom Host from day one, three illusions, and a d20 to strike until level three — let the host do the hitting.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Nothing under 5 hp will come near you, and anything with 20 hit points or more comes straight at you — and gets there first. You have been made important by the only creatures whose vote counts: the large ones.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Plus two with every weapon ever forged, plus three with anything you have repaired yourself. You cannot parley — you attack creatures without question, literally — and once a fight has your scent there is no clean exit in round one either. The book files this under abilities.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You never speak — literally; no fluency, no encounter, ever talks you out of a fight. Your opening strike lands for maximum damage and after that a 1 or a 2 opens something up. The silence isn't a vow, it's a tactic.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You take a percentage of everything: purses, shop stock, treasure nobody has opened yet. You have never been caught, but every shopkeeper in the maze remembers your face all the same — a quarter more to buy from them, a quarter less when you sell. You have never been thanked either.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Traps disarm themselves in your presence and no sealed room has ever held you. Your hands, though, can't leave a magic ring, amulet or cloak alone — use one and, about one time in twenty, it comes apart right there for a d10 of your own hp and is dust. Potions and scrolls you handle like anyone else.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: A magical katana, armour like plate, and enough clatter that you never win the first roll of anything. You never run. The book uses the word suicidal and does not soften it.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You take criticals on a 2 and deal them never. Serve to skill level III and they knight you, which is the army conceding that the first three levels were a waste of you.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Two dozen spells to start and two more each level, nearly all of it fire, with a one-in-eight chance per level of simply forgetting the ones that aren't. Your arm caps out at 9 damage. Nobody hired the arm.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: You can call something up from your very first day. Everything you call arrives twice as strong and twice as long-lived, and one time in eight it arrives on the wrong side. The book declines to say whose fault that is.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Evil, and productive with it — a potion copied every day and a standing bonus to every walking dead thing in the room. The dead don't know you're helping. You haven't told them.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: Every school of magic, and a flat refusal to teach anybody who isn't an Apprentice. You will not raise a hand while an attack spell is left in the book; once the book cannot hurt anything, the staff will do. Two wizards in a party fight each other; there is only one of you, which helps.

entries.trigger: the sub-class blurb (roller and Hero tab)
texts: No mail, no plate — the store won't offer it and your own hands won't take it — no shield, and a quarter staff you are genuinely superb with. You speak to every animal in here except dragons — a pity, as it is mostly dragons that want a word.
+2 damage and 1 hp/day upkeep; foes strike at a better die; armor wears at half the rate; being small makes it one face harder to hit.
Strikes a die better and hits on 5 whatever the class — but thin-boned and easy to hit, and being small costs it 2 damage.
Never wears armor, strikes last, frenzies into a second wild swing that never wastes itself on a corpse; thick hide soaks 2 from every blow.
No advantages, no penalties. The dungeon's default.
75 hp regardless of class and +11 damage (being large adds 2), but eats two rations a night and is one face easier to hit.
Heals twice as fast, learns half as quickly. Magic Users despise them.

Where this prototype departs from the rulebook

Every weapon, armour value, creature, spell, potion, trap, encounter, climb and leap now comes from the rulebook itself. This page lists only the places the prototype knowingly departs from it — the list to reconcile if you ever revise the PDF.

Encounters roll themselves and "who gets it" always gets you. Party-only rules are therefore inert: the Cutthroat murdering a companion, the Court Mage's angry party members, two Wizards refusing to share a room, the Knight drawing fire off the group, an elf boosting morale.

, one returning every 20 squares, instead of once per 100 squares. The book's cadence is a party's pace, not one caster's.
Magic Users start at 25 + d10 hp
rather than a flat 25. Twenty-five with no armour is one bad round, every time.
Elves keep 0.6 of their Hit Points
, not half. A flat half on a 25-hp caster was a death sentence; the other elven rules are as written.
Trolls eat two rations a night
on top of the 15 hp cost of living. Otherwise 75 hp and +9 damage carried no real price.
Every Thief opens with a backstab
. The class description is three-quarters stealth and back-stabbing, and the rules gave it no mechanic.

and clear with a night's rest. As written they run at up to 2d6 a square with only a Cure spell to stop them — which no solo delver has. They still take everything you had.
